passage: A parent who hears a child begin a sentence in one language and finish it in another often worries that the child has learned neither properly. Teachers have voiced the same anxiety, and so, at times, have bilingual speakers themselves, who describe their own mixing with a kind of apology, as though it betrayed a laziness they ought to overcome. The assumption behind the worry is simple: a speaker who switches must be reaching for a word he does not have, and a speaker who is constantly reaching has not finished learning.

The assumption is not absurd, and sometimes it is true. Anyone who has lived between two languages knows the moment when the word for a kitchen utensil, or for a form at the bank, has been acquired in one language and simply not in the other. But careful recordings of bilingual conversation suggest that such gaps account for only part of what happens, and not the most interesting part. Switches tend to fall at points where the grammars of the two languages fit together and to avoid points where they clash, so that a sentence begun in one language and finished in another is usually well formed by the standards of both. A speaker who was merely groping for words would not be so tidy. To switch in this way, one needs to know two grammars well enough to sense, without thinking, where they can be joined.

Nor is the timing of a switch random. Speakers move into the other language to report what someone else said, to mark a change of topic, to soften a refusal, to signal that a remark is a joke, or to draw a listener in or shut one out. A grandmother's proverb may be quoted in the language she used, not because the speaker cannot translate it, but because the translation would lose the grandmother. In such uses the switch itself carries meaning, much as a change of tone does within a single language; it is a resource that monolingual speakers lack, not a failure that they have avoided.

None of this means that every setting must welcome mixing. An examination set in one language, or a document that must be read by people who know only one, may reasonably require a speaker to stay within it, and a bilingual who could not do so would indeed have a problem. The error lies in treating the ability to keep languages apart as the measure of competence, and the habit of combining them as its absence. Most bilinguals can do both. Judging them by the first alone is like judging a pianist only by whether she can play with one hand.

options.A: Praising a novelist for freely mixing genres even when readers report that the resulting books are hard to follow.
options.B: Judging a chess player only by her results in fast games, while ignoring her long and strong record in slow, classical games.
options.C: Requiring a surgeon to use only the instruments approved for a particular operation, although she is equally skilled with several others.
options.D: Grading a musician trained in two traditions only on how strictly she keeps them apart, and treating her blending of the two as poor training.

passage: When a welfare benefit goes unclaimed by many of the people entitled to it, the usual explanation is that they did not know about it, did not need it badly enough or could not be bothered. The explanation locates the problem in the claimant. It rarely asks what claiming actually involves: discovering that the benefit exists, working out whether one qualifies, gathering documents that may be held by three different offices, completing a form whose questions assume a settled address and a regular income, and then, often, doing it all again a few months later to prove that nothing has changed.

These demands are usually described as administrative friction, an unfortunate but neutral by-product of running any large programme. They are not neutral. Every hour required to claim is an hour that some people can spare more easily than others, and the people least able to spare it are frequently those the programme was meant to help: the seriously ill, those working irregular shifts, those for whom scarcity has already consumed much of the attention that form-filling demands. A requirement that costs a comfortable applicant an afternoon may cost a struggling one the benefit itself.

There is a further reason to look closely at such burdens. Because they are set through forms, procedures and office hours rather than through legislation, they can change who receives a benefit without any public decision that it should. A government that wished to spend less on a programme but did not wish to say so could add a document to the list or shorten the period for renewal, and the number of recipients would fall while the rules of entitlement stayed exactly as they were. Whether or not anyone intends this, the effect is a form of policy made out of sight, insulated from the debate that a change in the law would provoke.

This is not to say that verification is illegitimate. Public programmes depend on the belief that money goes to those entitled to it, and some checking sustains that belief among the taxpayers who fund them. But the costs of checking are borne in two places, in the office and in the lives of applicants, and only the first tends to be counted. A sound design would weigh the time and strain imposed on claimants as seriously as the cost of the errors it prevents, and would treat a large gap between entitlement and receipt as evidence about the system rather than about the people outside it.

options.A: A requirement that is a minor nuisance for one applicant may be decisive for another applicant.
options.B: The costs of verification fall partly on applicants, and these are often left out of the reckoning.
options.C: Burdens on claimants are introduced chiefly by governments that want to cut spending without public debate.
options.D: A fall in the number of people receiving a benefit need not reflect any change in the rules that define who is entitled to it.

passage: Virtue ethics asks not what rule an action follows or what outcome it produces but what kind of person performs it. Its central concepts are traits of character such as honesty, courage and compassion, conceived as stable dispositions that lead a person to act well across a wide range of circumstances. The compassionate person does not help only when it is convenient or when someone is watching; her compassion shows itself in the market and at home, towards friends and towards strangers. It is this breadth that distinguishes a virtue from a habit, and it is what makes the attribution of a virtue a substantial claim about a person rather than a summary of what she happened to do last week.

In recent decades a group of critics, often called situationists, has argued that this picture is empirically naive. They point to a body of experimental work in social psychology, some of it now disputed, which has been taken to show that small and morally irrelevant features of a situation, such as whether a person is in a hurry or in a pleasant mood, predict whether she will help someone in need far better than anything we know about her character. If behaviour is driven so heavily by circumstance, the critics conclude, then broad traits of the kind virtue ethics requires are rare or nonexistent, and a theory built around them describes a psychology that human beings do not have. On this view, to call someone honest or kind is less a discovery about her than a story we tell to make her conduct look more orderly than it is.

The argument is more damaging to some versions of virtue ethics than to others. If the theory claimed that most people possess the virtues, the evidence would tell heavily against it. But the classical tradition never claimed this. It held that full virtue is difficult, uncommon and achieved, if at all, through long training, and that most people are a mixture of good impulses and weak resolve. Evidence that ordinary people are easily swayed by circumstance is exactly what such a tradition would predict. Indeed, much of the advice it offers, to avoid temptations rather than trust oneself to resist them and to choose one's companions with care, makes sense only on the assumption that character is fragile.

This reply, however, has a cost that its defenders do not always acknowledge. If genuine virtue is so rare that experimental samples almost never contain it, then virtue ethics can no longer claim the advantage it has often advertised over its rivals: that it describes moral life as it is actually lived, in terms of real people and their recognisable qualities. An ideal that almost no one embodies may still be worth pursuing, but it begins to look less like a description of character and more like a rule of the kind the theory set out to replace, a standard against which conduct is measured rather than a source from which it flows.

The situationist challenge, then, does not refute virtue ethics, but it changes what the theory can coherently promise. The theory can keep its account of the ideal, or its claim to realism about ordinary people, but it is hard to see how it can keep both. Which it should give up is a question that experiments alone cannot answer, since it depends on what we want an ethical theory to do: to guide those who aspire to goodness, or to describe those whose characters are already formed.

options.A: A rulebook for a game can be replaced without loss by a description of how skilled players actually behave in matches.
options.B: A recipe that usually fails when beginners attempt it must have been written incorrectly by the cook who devised it.
options.C: A training programme grows more effective the more often its trainees repeat each of the exercises it prescribes.
options.D: A map can be drawn to show the route an expert ought to take or to record the paths walkers actually use, but hardly to do both at once.

passage: Arguments about gentrification tend to collapse into a single question: are the people who lived in a neighbourhood forced out when wealthier newcomers arrive? The question has the merit of being answerable, at least in principle. One can follow households over time, count how many leave, and compare the rate with that in neighbourhoods that have not changed. Suppose such a count found that long-standing residents of a gentrifying district left no faster than residents of similar districts elsewhere. Many would conclude that the harm of gentrification had been exaggerated, and that what remained of the complaint was mere nostalgia.

That conclusion would be premature, because it assumes that the only way to lose a neighbourhood is to leave it. Consider the resident who stays. The grocer who extended credit has been replaced by a shop whose prices assume another income; the bench outside it, once a place to sit for an afternoon, now draws the attention of a security guard; the park is the same park, but the conduct expected in it has quietly changed, and complaints to the police now come from people she does not know, about behaviour that was ordinary a decade ago. She has not moved, and no count of departures will register her, yet the place in which she lives has been withdrawn from her as surely as if she had. To call this nostalgia is to mistake a loss of standing for a loss of scenery.

The difficulty is that the language best suited to describing this loss, the language of a neighbourhood's 'character', is also the language most readily turned to the opposite purpose. Affluent districts invoke their character to resist new housing, to keep out flats that might bring poorer residents, to preserve a streetscape that functions, whatever its owners intend, as a barrier. If character means the look of the buildings and the tone of the streets, then the long-standing resident and the exclusionary homeowner are making the same argument, and it is not one that deserves much sympathy.

The way out is to locate character not in the fabric of a place but in the relations it sustains: who is able to use it, on what terms, and with what claim to be heard. On this view, what the staying resident has lost is not a familiar shopfront but the practical standing she once had in her own street, and what the exclusionary homeowner defends is not a set of relations at all but the absence of people who might form new ones. The distinction will not settle every case, and it asks more of planners than a count of departures does. But it allows us to take the quieter harms of gentrification seriously without lending our sympathy to every resident who would prefer that nothing near them ever changed.

options.A: A resident who stays in a gentrifying district loses more of her neighbourhood than one who is forced to leave it.
options.B: The same appeal to a neighbourhood's character can serve both to describe a genuine loss and to justify exclusion.
options.C: Judging character by the relations a place sustains demands more of planners than counting those who leave.
options.D: A count of departures, however careful, cannot register the losses of residents who remain in a changing district.

passage: A respectable argument holds that negative criticism of new books is a waste of everyone's time. So many books are published each year that no critic can notice more than a sliver of them; the space a journal devotes to criticism is therefore precious, and to spend it explaining why a book is bad is to deny it to a book that deserves attention. On this view the most damning verdict a critic can deliver is silence. A poor book left unmentioned simply sinks, and nothing is lost except the pleasure that some critics take in wounding. The position has the further appeal of seeming kind, which is no small recommendation in a literary world where writers and critics are often the same people.

The argument is tidy, but it quietly assumes that the only job of criticism is to guide readers in choosing what to read. If that were so, the notice of a weak book would indeed be wasted, since a reader who is told merely to skip something has learned nothing that he could use elsewhere. But criticism has always done something besides sorting. A careful account of why a book fails is also an account of what success would have looked like, and in giving it the critic makes public a set of standards that readers can test, dispute and apply for themselves. The reader who follows a well-argued case against a novel he admired may end unconvinced, yet he will read the next novel more alertly.

There is a further cost to silence. If critics write only about the books they admire, praise becomes the sole currency of criticism, and like any currency issued without limit it loses its value. A notice that can only ever say yes tells the reader very little, because its enthusiasm is not the outcome of a judgement that could have gone the other way. Readers soon learn to discount it, as they discount the admiring phrases printed on the cover of every new book, and the critic whose praise is sincere is then heard no more clearly than the publicist. The possibility of dispraise is what gives praise its meaning.

None of this licenses cruelty, and the case for restraint does have force in one kind of instance. A modest first novel from a small press, which few people will encounter anyway, gains nothing from a public demolition, and neither do its readers. The negative notice earns its space when the book in question is prominent: widely praised, heavily promoted, or likely to shape what others write. There the critic who dissents is not kicking someone who is down but contesting a reputation that is already shaping public taste, and that is among the most useful things criticism can do.

options.A: Critics take more pleasure in writing unfavourable notices than favourable ones.
options.B: A poor book that is ignored will sell fewer copies than one that is attacked in print.
options.C: Most of the books published each year are of poor quality and deserve no attention.
options.D: Criticism exists solely to help readers decide which books are worth their time.

passage: When an automated system fails and a human operator fails to rescue it, the official account usually ends with the words 'human error'. The phrase is accurate in a narrow sense, since a person did do the wrong thing, but it hides the way the situation was produced. Automation is typically introduced to take over the parts of a task that are routine and well understood. What remains for the human is whatever the designers could not automate: the rare, ambiguous, fast-moving situations in which the machine gives up or behaves strangely. The person is thus left with the hardest part of the job, and is expected to perform it suddenly, after long periods of doing almost nothing.

Those long periods matter. Skill at controlling a process is kept alive by exercising it, and an operator who has spent months watching a screen rather than flying, steering or adjusting will have less of it than one who did the work by hand. Worse, the automation removes the everyday experience through which people build an intuitive model of how the system behaves, so that when something goes wrong they must reason about it from first principles, under pressure, with alarms sounding. Monitoring is also something human beings do badly. Attention drifts when nothing happens for hours, and the more reliable the machine, the longer the stretches in which nothing happens.

The result is a curious inversion. The better the automation works in ordinary conditions, the less prepared its human supervisors may be for the extraordinary ones, and the more surprising their failure will look when it comes. Calling that failure human error locates the fault in the individual at the very moment when the design of the whole arrangement deserves scrutiny.

None of this is a case against automation, which has removed a great deal of tedium and many kinds of mistake. It is a case for designing automated systems around the people who must step in when they fail. That might mean having operators run the process manually at regular intervals so that their skill does not decay, building displays that show what the machine is doing and why rather than only whether it is working, or deciding deliberately that some tasks should remain shared even when they could be fully automated. Such measures cost efficiency in the short run. Their justification is that the moments they prepare for, although rare, are the ones in which the most is at stake.

options.A: Attention drifts when nothing happens for long stretches, and a reliable machine makes such stretches longer.
options.B: They trust the machine so completely that they decide there is no longer any need to watch it closely.
options.C: The displays they watch are usually too complicated to be read quickly when an emergency arises.
options.D: They have been given less training than the operators who used to do the work by hand.

passage: Spoken irony rarely needs announcing. A slight drag on a word, a flattened pitch, a pause before the punchline: listeners pick up such cues without noticing that they have done so, and the speaker relies on them without noticing either. Writing, however expressive in other respects, strips most of them away. For centuries this mattered less than it might have, because the written forms people used for personal exchange, letters above all, were slow, composed and long enough to establish their own tone over several paragraphs. A letter writer who wished to be ironic had room to prepare the reader for it.

The short typed message removes that room while keeping the pace of speech. Exchanges happen in seconds, between people who often know each other well enough to joke, in fragments too brief to carry their own context. The result is a familiar variety of communicative accident. A remark meant as affectionate teasing arrives as a rebuke; a dry agreement reads as sincere enthusiasm, or the reverse. The writer, who heard the intended tone in his own head as he typed, is often the last to see that it was not on the screen.

Writers have not, however, accepted this deprivation quietly. Over the past few decades they have built, without any committee to guide them, a supplementary system of signals: the small faces and symbols that can be appended to a sentence, the strategic use of capitals and repeated letters, even the presence or absence of a full stop, which among some groups of writers has come to make a short reply sound curt. It is common to lament these devices as a decline in the standards of written language. That complaint misses what they are for. They are not a lazy substitute for vocabulary but a written prosody, an attempt to restore precisely the cues that typing removed.

Yet the new system has a weakness that spoken prosody largely lacks. The meaning of a rising tone is shared across most speakers of a language; the meaning of a particular symbol or a missing full stop is settled within smaller circles and changes quickly. A face that one group uses to soften a criticism may strike another as mocking, and a message read across a gap of age or community can misfire precisely because the writer took care to mark its tone. The invention of written prosody, in other words, has not abolished misreading so much as relocated it, from the gap between voice and text to the gap between the conventions of different readers.

options.A: critical, because the view mistakes devices for restoring tone for mere carelessness.
options.B: neutral, because the author reports the view without indicating any judgement about it.
options.C: approving, because the author regards the signals as too local and unstable to count as a proper part of written language.
options.D: sympathetic, because the author agrees that the signals are less precise than a well-chosen word.

passage: The defence of meritocracy rests on a simple and appealing idea: that positions and rewards should go to those who earn them, through talent and effort, rather than to those born into the right family. Against the background of aristocratic privilege this was a revolutionary thought, and it remains a powerful one. Yet it has been attacked, with increasing force, on the ground that talent and effort are themselves largely matters of luck. No one chooses the abilities they are born with. And the capacity to work hard, to persist through failure and to defer gratification, is shaped by upbringing, health and circumstance in ways that no one controls. If this is so, the critic concludes, nobody deserves the rewards that meritocracy hands out, and the language of merit is a flattering fiction.

The premises of this argument are difficult to deny, but its conclusion moves too fast. It runs together two different claims that a person might make about a reward. One is that she deserves it in a deep moral sense, that the world would be unjust if she did not have it. The other is that she is entitled to it, because she has met the conditions that a fair set of rules laid down in advance. A runner who wins a race under fair conditions is entitled to the prize even if her speed owes much to her genes and her coaching; to take the prize away on the ground that she was lucky would itself be a wrong, because she trained and competed on the understanding that winning would bring it. Entitlement of this kind does not depend on the winner being the author of her own talents. It depends only on the fairness of the rules and her compliance with them.

Seen in this light, a society can reward productive contributions, and honour the expectations its rules create, without pretending that the rewards measure the moral worth of those who receive them. It also leaves open, as it should, the question of whether the rules themselves are fair, including how much inequality of reward they ought to permit. What the luck argument undermines is not the practice of rewarding achievement but a particular story told about it, the story in which the successful have simply earned their place and the unsuccessful have simply failed to earn theirs. That story is corrosive. It encourages the winners to regard their advantages as wholly their own, and it adds to the losers' material disadvantage the further injury of being told that they deserved it. The remedy is not to abolish merit but to hold it more lightly.

options.A: A runner who finished second insists that she deserved the prize more than the winner because she trained harder.
options.B: A firm abolishes all bonuses because its managers conclude that performance is mostly a matter of good luck.
options.C: A lottery winner has a valid claim to the jackpot under the rules of the draw, though nobody thinks she earned it.
options.D: A worker paid less than a colleague for the same work complains that the firm's pay scale is unfair to her.

passage: Suppose the history of life could be rewound to some early point and allowed to run again. Would anything like the present living world appear a second time? One school answers no. Evolution, on this view, is a chain of contingencies, each step dependent on the particular steps before it and on unrepeatable accidents of climate, geology and mutation. Alter any early link, and the chain would run off in another direction entirely; the existence of vertebrates, of flowering plants or of our own species would be no more to be expected than a particular sequence of cards in a shuffled deck. On this view the tree of life is a record of accidents, intelligible after the fact but not predictable before it, and any search for a direction in it reads our own presence back into a history that never had us in mind. The rival school points to the remarkable frequency with which evolution arrives at the same solution independently. Camera-like eyes have arisen separately in vertebrates and in octopuses; streamlined bodies have evolved in fish, in extinct marine reptiles and in dolphins; flight has been achieved by insects, pterosaurs, birds and bats. If the same designs keep recurring, the argument runs, the outcome of a second run would be broadly familiar.

Each school has a strong case, and each tends to treat the other's evidence as anecdote. Convergence enthusiasts can list hundreds of cases, but the list is assembled after the fact from the solutions that did recur, and it says nothing about the far larger number of forms that appeared once and never again. Contingency enthusiasts can point to those unrepeated forms, but they often treat the mere fact that a lineage had a particular history as proof that its outcome depended on that history, which does not follow: a ball may take a unique path down a hillside and still come to rest in the only hollow at the bottom.

Much of the disagreement, I want to suggest, dissolves once we notice that the two schools are describing life at different levels of detail. At the level of broad functional solutions, a second run would very probably produce organisms that see, swim, fly and filter food, because the physical problems of moving through water or air, or of forming an image from light, admit only a few good solutions. At the level of particular lineages, the replay would almost certainly differ: there is no reason to expect that the flying creatures would be birds, or that the swimmers would have backbones. Convergence is a claim about the space of workable designs; contingency is a claim about which occupants of that space history happens to supply. The two are compatible, and both are probably true.

This reconciliation has a cost, and it is worth stating plainly. If the question that matters is whether a replay would produce something like us, a self-aware animal that makes tools and uses language, then neither school's best evidence is decisive. Intelligence of our kind has arisen, so far as we know, only once, and a single case cannot reveal whether it was a likely destination or a fluke. The recurrence of eyes and wings tells us that some problems have few solutions; it does not tell us that every capacity we value is among those solutions. On the questions that most excite the public, the honest answer is that the evidence does not yet discriminate between the two views.

options.A: the history of a lineage is of no use in understanding what that lineage became.
options.B: the outcomes of evolution are fixed in advance by the physical shape of the environment.
options.C: contingency enthusiasts are wrong to claim that many forms appeared only once.
options.D: an end point reached by a route no one could repeat may still have been very likely to be reached.

passage: It is easy to write the history of urban smell as a simple story of progress. Pre-modern cities stank of sewage, tanneries, slaughterhouses and unwashed bodies; reformers built drains and water supplies; the stench retreated. Every part of this is true, and anyone inclined to romanticise the crowded streets of earlier centuries should be reminded of it. But the story assumes that the nose is a constant instrument, registering the same smells with the same disgust in every age, and that assumption does not survive a reading of the sources.

Residents of older towns certainly complained about smells, but their complaints were selective. Odours that later generations would find unbearable, such as the smell of a dung heap beside a house, were often accepted as part of ordinary life, while others, associated with particular trades or with neighbours who were disliked, drew sustained protest. What made a smell intolerable depended less on its strength than on what it was thought to mean. And from the late eighteenth century onwards, in much of Europe, smells came to carry a very specific meaning with new urgency. Under the old theory that disease spread through foul air, now taken up by physicians and reformers, a bad smell was not merely unpleasant; it was a warning, perhaps even the danger itself.

The theory was wrong, but it was productive. Because it identified smell with sickness, it gave reformers a reason, and a sense of urgency, to remove the sources of smell, and many of the measures they took, from covered sewers to the regular removal of refuse, did reduce disease, though for reasons they did not understand. A mistaken idea about how illness spread thus helped to justify works whose real benefit lay elsewhere. When the germ theory displaced it, smell lost its medical authority; it did not lose its power.

Freed from medicine, the vocabulary of smell attached itself more firmly to persons. Middle-class households that had learned to fear foul air now learned to fear the odour of the poor, the newcomer and the manual worker, and the judgement passed easily from bodies to character. The cleaner cities became, the more a lingering smell could serve as a mark of social distance. This is why a history of smell cannot be only a history of drains; it must also be a history of who was allowed to call whom offensive, and of how a sense that seems the most immediate of all has always been schooled.

options.A: came from the drains and sewers that reformers had recently built to carry waste away from the streets.
options.B: was linked in residents' minds with a particular trade or with neighbours they disliked.
options.C: was believed by physicians to carry disease, since every bad smell was then treated as a medical danger.
options.D: was stronger than the ordinary smells of household refuse and animal dung that residents lived beside.

passage: Economists who agree that carbon emissions should carry a price often disagree, sometimes heatedly, about how the price should be set. One camp prefers a tax: the government announces a charge per tonne of emissions and leaves firms to decide how much to cut. The other prefers a cap with tradable permits: the government fixes the total quantity of emissions allowed, issues permits for that amount, and lets trading among firms determine what a permit costs. In a world without uncertainty the two would be equivalent. Any cap implies some price at which permits would trade, and any tax implies some level to which emissions would fall; a regulator who knew the costs of abatement could reach the same outcome by either route.

The difference appears once we admit that no one knows those costs in advance. A tax fixes the price and leaves the quantity uncertain: if cutting emissions proves harder than expected, firms will pay the tax and emit more than was planned. A cap fixes the quantity and leaves the price uncertain: if cutting proves harder, permit prices will climb, perhaps steeply. Which uncertainty is more tolerable depends on the shape of the damage. If each additional tonne does roughly the same harm as the last, a fixed price tracks the damage well and a volatile price merely adds cost. If harm accelerates sharply past some threshold, a fixed quantity matters more than a stable price. Because the harm from carbon depends on the stock accumulated in the atmosphere over decades rather than on any single year's emissions, many economists conclude that year-to-year overshoots matter little and that a tax, or something that behaves like one, is the better instrument.

Advocates of trading reply that this argument, persuasive in the seminar room, neglects politics. A cap states its environmental goal openly, which can make it easier to defend, and the free allocation of permits to affected industries, though it hands them a windfall, has often been the price of getting a scheme adopted at all. A tax, by contrast, announces a cost to every voter and invites a fresh campaign against it with every scheduled rise.

The more telling fact is that, in practice, the two designs have drifted towards each other. Trading schemes have acquired price floors, to keep permits from becoming nearly worthless when demand falls, and price ceilings, to stop them from spiking; taxes have been given scheduled increases linked to emissions targets. The resulting hybrids are neither pure price nor pure quantity. This convergence suggests that the long debate was, in part, a debate about labels. What decides whether a carbon price works is less whether it is called a tax or a cap than whether it is high enough, broad enough in what it covers, and credible enough that firms invest on the expectation that it will last.

options.A: either instrument equally well, since a regulator who chose the right level could reach the same outcome by both.
options.B: a fixed charge per unit discharged, since the harm depends on what accumulates over decades and not on any one season.
options.C: a limit on the total quantity discharged, since keeping below the threshold matters more than a predictable cost.
options.D: a limit on discharges paired with a ceiling on the permit price, since that keeps costs predictable if cutting proves hard.

passage: The usual story of standard time is a story of order arriving to rescue confusion. Before the railways, we are told, every town kept its own time, set by the sun at its highest point, so that a clock in one town might differ by several minutes from a clock in another only a short distance to the west. Travellers were bewildered, timetables were impossible, and the adoption of uniform zones was simply common sense finally asserting itself. The story is not false, but it misdescribes what was replaced.

Local solar time was not a muddle for the people who used it. It was tied to something everyone could see: the sun reached its highest point at noon, and noon meant the same thing in the market, the place of worship and the field. For a community whose dealings were mostly with itself, there was little need to coordinate with anyone else, and a time that matched the daylight was the most sensible time to keep. The differences between towns became a problem only when goods and people began to move between them quickly enough for a few minutes to matter.

That is what the railways did. A train leaving one town and arriving at another an hour later could not be scheduled sensibly if each station kept its own noon, and on single tracks a mismatch of a few minutes could put two trains on the same stretch of line. Railway companies therefore began keeping a single time along their routes, and governments eventually followed them, dividing territories into broad bands within which every clock agreed. The change was not everywhere welcomed, and some towns resented being told that noon now arrived when a distant company declared that it had. Within each band, clock noon and solar noon could now differ noticeably, and in places at the edges of a zone they still do.

Nothing here suggests that standard time was a mistake. Coordinated schedules saved lives on the railways and made later systems, from telegraph networks to air traffic, workable. The point is that standardisation was not the discovery of a correct time hidden beneath local error. It was a choice to make clocks answer to a network rather than to the sky, made because the network had become more important to daily life than the position of the sun. To call the older arrangement confusion is to judge it by the needs of a world that had not yet arrived.

options.A: A way of setting clocks should be judged by how well it suits the needs of those who keep it, not by its closeness to a true time.
options.B: Standard time corrected errors in local timekeeping that small towns had failed to notice because they traded mainly with themselves.
options.C: Once the railways had spread, the position of the sun ceased to have any importance for daily life.
options.D: Solar time is the true time, and standard time is merely a convenient approximation that the railways adopted for their own purposes.

passage: Discussions of the so-called file drawer problem usually begin with journals. Editors, the complaint runs, prefer results that show something: a drug that works, an effect that appears, a difference between groups. Studies that find nothing are harder to place, and so they remain in researchers' filing cabinets while the published literature fills up with positive findings. A reader who surveys that literature will then overestimate how often, and how strongly, the effect in question occurs, since the failures that would have tempered the estimate never reached print. The literature, in other words, is not a sample of the research that was done but a selection from it, made on the very quantity that readers most want to estimate.

There is truth in this account, and the remedy it suggests, journals that commit in advance to publishing well-conducted studies whatever they find, deserves the support it has received. But the account places the drawer in the wrong office. Ask a working scientist what became of her last inconclusive experiment and the answer is seldom that an editor turned it down. More often it was never written up at all. The study was abandoned before any journal had a chance to reject it, and it sits in the drawer because its own author put it there.

The reason is not laziness. A positive result, whatever its other defects, announces itself: something happened. A null result is mute about its own meaning. It may show that the effect does not exist, or that the sample was too small to detect it, or that a reagent was contaminated, or that a student misread the protocol. The researcher who obtained it is often the person least able to tell which, and the most honest description she could offer, that she looked and did not see, is one that few colleagues would think worth the trouble of reading. Writing such a paper costs weeks and earns little, and the decision to move on is, from where she stands, entirely rational.

If this is right, obliging journals to accept null results treats the symptom at the far end. The drawer will empty only when null results become informative, and that depends on decisions made before any data are collected: samples large enough that a real effect would probably have been seen, procedures specified in advance so that a failure cannot be blamed afterwards on improvisation, checks built in to show that the apparatus was working. A null result obtained under such conditions says something definite, and researchers will publish it for the same reason they publish anything, because it tells their colleagues something they did not know.

options.A: she fears that publishing it would contradict the published findings of senior colleagues in her field.
options.B: editors have made it clear in advance that they will not consider studies that find no effect.
options.C: she herself often cannot tell what the absence of the expected effect actually means.
options.D: she is too occupied with newer projects to spend time on work that has already failed.

passage: Theories of punishment have long been divided between those that look forward and those that look back. Forward-looking theories justify punishment by its effects: it deters, it incapacitates, perhaps it reforms. Their persistent embarrassment is that they seem to license too much. If the point of punishment were simply to discourage crime, then punishing an innocent person whom the public believed guilty might serve that point as well as punishing the guilty one, and sometimes better, since it would be quicker. Most people regard this conclusion as monstrous, which suggests that the effects of punishment, however important, cannot be the whole of its justification.

An expressive theory offers to supply what is missing. On this view punishment is, before anything else, a form of communication: the community's way of declaring that an act was wrong and that the person who did it is answerable for it. This explains at once why the innocent may not be punished. To condemn someone who did nothing is not an inefficient use of punishment but a lie told in its language. It also explains why we distinguish a fine from a tax, though both take money: the tax carries no message of blame, while the fine carries little else.

The obvious objection is that condemnation can be expressed in words. If the point of a prison sentence is to say that an act was wrong, why not simply say so, in a formal judgement solemnly delivered? The expressive theorist's reply is that words alone are too cheap to carry the message. A declaration that costs the offender nothing would be heard as a declaration that the wrong did not matter much; only something that is felt as a burden registers the seriousness of what was done.

This reply is ingenious, but it has an uncomfortable implication. If hard treatment communicates because of the meanings a society attaches to it, then how much hard treatment is needed depends on those meanings, and meanings can drift. A society accustomed to long sentences will hear a short one as a shrug; the same sentence elsewhere might sound like thunder. The expressive theory, in other words, cannot by itself tell us how severe punishment should be, because severity is fixed by convention, and conventions can escalate without limit. That is not a reason to abandon the theory, which captures something the forward-looking view plainly misses. It is a reason to think that the theory needs a partner: some independent principle, perhaps of proportion or of humanity, that sets limits the language of condemnation cannot set for itself.

options.A: Where courts declare offenders guilty but impose no penalty, the public judges those offences as serious as ones punished by imprisonment.
options.B: Fines that are very small relative to an offender's wealth tend to be treated by offenders as a routine cost of doing business.
options.C: Long prison sentences do less to reduce reoffending than shorter sentences combined with close supervision after release.
options.D: Judges in different countries tend to deliver their verdicts in quite different styles and in very different forms of language.

passage: Architects tend to speak of a building as finished on the day it is handed over, and most architectural criticism shares the assumption. For its occupants, however, the handover is a beginning. Within a few years the first partitions have gone up or come down, a porch has been enclosed, a garage has become a bedroom, and the building has started to diverge from its drawings. A family grows and then shrinks, a business expands into the floor above, a school changes the way it teaches, and each of these shifts leaves its mark on the fabric. Over a century the divergence can be so complete that little of the original arrangement survives except the outer walls and the structural frame. If we want to know how well a building has been designed, the question of how it absorbs such changes deserves at least as much attention as the question of how it looked when new.

The obvious response is to design for change, and for several decades architects attempted exactly that. Offices and schools were built as open floors with movable partitions, and houses with walls that could slide, fold or be unbolted, so that occupants could rearrange the interior at will. The results were often disappointing. Movable partitions were seldom moved, because moving them was laborious and disturbed the services concealed within them; the flexible plan turned out to be a plan that suited no particular use well; and the occupants, rather than enjoying their freedom, filled the space with improvised screens and cabinets to make the rooms that the design had declined to provide. Designing for every possible use, it emerged, had been a way of designing for none.

The buildings that have in fact proved most adaptable are frequently ones that were never designed with change in mind. Old warehouses and mills, with their regular grids of columns, generous ceiling heights and thick, plain walls, have been turned into flats, studios, schools and offices with surprising ease. Terraced houses built for one family have been divided into apartments and, a generation later, joined up again. What these buildings share is not flexibility in the engineered sense but a kind of slack: dimensions a little larger than any one use required, a structure simple enough to be understood by ordinary builders, and surfaces that can be cut into without catastrophe. The ordinary builder called in to knock two rooms together can see at once where the loads run and what may safely be taken away. They fit their first use loosely, and that looseness is what lets them fit their later uses at all.

The lesson is an uncomfortable one for a profession that prides itself on precision. A building tailored exactly to its brief, every room sized to its programme and every service routed to suit it, is admirable on the day of opening and brittle thereafter, because the brief will change and the building cannot. Generosity of this kind costs something at the outset, in floor area and in height, and clients are seldom eager to pay for space that nobody has yet asked for. This is not an argument against all precision; an operating theatre or a laboratory must fit its use closely, and a little slack in the wrong place is merely waste. But for most ordinary buildings, which will outlive the purposes for which they were commissioned, the more durable virtue is a certain generosity, together with a willingness on the architect's part to regard the occupants' later alterations not as defacement but as the building continuing to do its job.

options.A: Flexible-plan offices built in recent decades have been demolished far more often than old warehouses in the same districts.
options.B: Some warehouses converted into flats were later returned to storage when the demand for housing in their district fell.
options.C: Warehouses with low ceilings and irregular columns proved as easy to convert as those with generous ceilings and regular grids.
options.D: Most warehouses and mills were built without the slightest expectation that people would one day live or work in them.

passage: An investigation that changes a law or ends a career is remembered for its result, and the result makes it look like a sound investment. The reporting behind it rarely looks that way while it is under way. A team may spend months requesting documents, cultivating reluctant sources and checking figures, only to discover at the end that the story cannot be stood up, or that it is smaller and duller than it seemed. No publication can know in advance which of its inquiries will succeed, so the cost of the one that does must also cover the many that quietly fail. Editors who have watched a promising inquiry collapse after half a year learn caution, and caution, in a publication under financial pressure, usually means fewer inquiries.

This uncertainty would matter less if the rewards of success flowed back to the publication that paid for it. Mostly they do not. Once a finding is published, rivals can report it within hours, and the citizens who benefit from a cleaner tendering process or a safer bridge are seldom the readers who bought the paper that exposed the problem. In the language economists use, the work produces benefits that spill over to people who did not pay for them, and goods of that kind tend to be supplied in smaller quantities than a society, if it could choose collectively, would want.

The most important of those benefits is also the least visible. Officials who know that their accounts might one day be examined behave differently from officials who are sure that they will not be. A local administration that expects a reporter to read its contracts has a reason to keep them clean, and the corruption that never takes place leaves no story behind it. The contractor who decides not to inflate an invoice, because a reporter once asked awkward questions about a neighbouring council, will never appear in any account of what journalism has achieved. Investigative journalism therefore works partly as a deterrent, and like other deterrents it is judged unfairly by its visible output; a quiet year may be evidence of its success rather than of its irrelevance.

Admirers of the form sometimes overstate its virtues. Investigations can be mistaken, and a reporter convinced of wrongdoing may read ambiguous evidence in only one direction, with real costs for the people named. Nor is every exposure a public service; some are driven more by rivalry or an appetite for scandal than by any public interest. But the case for supporting such work does not depend on its infallibility. It depends on presence. Deterrence works only if the possibility of scrutiny is continuous; a single celebrated exposure every decade, however brilliant, does less to discipline the powerful than a modest but permanent habit of looking. Those who fund journalism, whether readers, donors or the public purse, should therefore value a steady capacity for inquiry above the occasional prize-winning scoop.

passage: When people imagine an intelligent animal, they usually imagine something built on the plan of their own bodies: a large brain in the head that gathers information, makes decisions and issues commands to obedient limbs. The octopus is a standing challenge to that picture. Its evolutionary line separated from ours more than half a billion years ago, long before either lineage had anything resembling a complex brain, so whatever intelligence it now has was assembled independently. And it was assembled on a strikingly different plan, for more of the octopus's neurons lie in its arms than in its central brain.

The arrangement has consequences that can be observed. An octopus arm can carry out a sequence of movements, such as reaching towards an object and bending to draw it in, with little apparent direction from the centre, and an arm separated from the body will for a time continue to respond to touch and to grasp what it meets. Each arm, it seems, handles much of the detail of its own movement, while the central brain sets broader goals. Instead of a commander and its troops, the better image might be a coordinator working with partners that each know their own business.

Popular writing has been quick to turn this into a slogan, describing the octopus as an animal with nine brains, or as a colony of minds sharing one body. The slogan goes too far. The arms are not independent agents with purposes of their own; they share a body, a nervous system and, in ordinary life, a single course of action, and the animal behaves as one creature pursuing one end at a time. What the anatomy shows is not that the octopus is many minds but that one mind can be organised so that much of its work is done at the edges.

That is the real lesson, and it reaches beyond octopuses. Much thinking about intelligence, in animals and in machines alike, has assumed that it must be centralised: that there must be some single place where everything comes together and is decided. The octopus suggests that centralisation is one solution among several, suited to some bodies and not to others. An animal with eight flexible arms and no skeleton faces a control problem that no single centre could easily solve, since each arm can bend at any point along its length and in any direction. Handing much of the work to the arms may be less an evolutionary curiosity than a sensible answer to the body the animal actually has.

options.B: the difficulty, for any single centre, of controlling flexible and boneless limbs that can bend at any point.
options.C: the very long period during which the octopus lineage has evolved apart from vertebrates.
options.D: the advantage to an animal that often loses arms of having limbs that can go on acting on their own.

passage: It has become a commonplace, in philosophy as much as in popular psychology, that a self is a kind of story. On this view a person is not a thing that persists beneath her experiences but the narrative she composes from them: the account of where she came from, what she has struggled against and where she is heading. The claim is usually advanced in two forms at once. The descriptive form says that human beings do in fact understand themselves through stories. The normative form adds that they ought to, and that a life which cannot be gathered into a coherent narrative is in some way impoverished or broken.

The descriptive claim is plausible for many people, but its generality is doubtful. Some people report that they do not experience their lives as a plot at all. They feel little connection with the person they were a decade ago, find the invitation to tell their life story faintly baffling, and live with their attention fixed on present tasks and relationships. Nor is there any obvious sense in which their lives go worse: they form attachments, deliberate carefully and take responsibility for their conduct, only without experiencing their existence as an unfolding plot. It would be rash to assume that such people are simply unreflective, or that they are concealing a narrative they would rather not acknowledge. Their testimony is at least as credible as that of people who say the opposite, and it suggests that narrative self-understanding is one way of being a self rather than the condition of being one.

The normative claim is more troubling. Stories have shapes, and the pressure to give one's life a shape is a pressure to select. Episodes that fit the arc are remembered and retold; those that do not are discarded or reinterpreted. Autobiographical memory is already reconstructive, and a governing narrative supplies it with a principle of selection that is rarely examined. A person who has told herself for years that she is someone who overcomes adversity will find it difficult to see the occasions on which she gave up, and harder still to learn from them. The demand for coherence can thus become a demand for a flattering kind of forgetting. A novelist may legitimately omit whatever does not serve the plot; a life conducted on the same principle may lose precisely the evidence it most needs.

None of this means that narrative has no place. Making a promise requires regarding one's future self as continuous with one's present intention, and recovering from bereavement or injury often involves finding a way to tell what happened so that it can be lived with. Understanding other people, too, frequently depends on grasping the story they take themselves to be in. These are genuine goods, and a person who could never assemble any part of her past into an account would be at a real disadvantage.

But the goods enumerated here are those of an instrument, not of an essence. We use stories to bind ourselves, to heal and to understand, and we can use them well or badly, often or seldom. To say that the self simply is its story makes the instrument indispensable, and it turns a difference in temperament into a deficiency. The more modest view leaves room both for lives that are lived largely in the present and for the episodes that refuse to fit, and it may well be the more truthful of the two.

options.D: explains differences of temperament between people as the outcome of the better or worse life stories they have told.

passage: When two experts disagree about a question the rest of us cannot assess, it can seem that the layperson has only two options: to become an expert herself, or to pick a side at random. Neither is attractive. The first is usually impossible within the time available, and the second makes a mockery of the idea that belief should answer to evidence. But the dilemma is false. Although the layperson cannot judge the dispute directly, she can often judge the disputants, and judgements of that kind can be reasonable even when the subject matter remains opaque to her.

Several kinds of evidence are available. She can ask whether either expert has a record of predictions that can be checked, and how those predictions fared. She can ask whether one of them stands to gain from being believed, through money, reputation or loyalty to an institution. She can ask how the rest of the field divides, bearing in mind that a majority counts for more when its members reached their views independently than when they all learned them from the same teacher. None of these questions requires understanding the dispute itself. Each concerns the circumstances in which a claim is advanced rather than its technical content, and each can be answered, at least roughly, by an attentive citizen with no specialised training whatever.

One tempting source of evidence is less useful than it looks. Laypeople often favour the expert who argues more fluently, answers objections more quickly and seems more at ease. Yet these are skills of performance, and they are only loosely connected with being right. A careful scientist may hedge, pause and admit uncertainties that a confident charlatan would brush aside, and an audience that rewards confidence is, in effect, rewarding the very habit that should make it suspicious. The difficulty is compounded by the fact that public debate, with its brief exchanges and its appetite for memorable phrases, is arranged almost entirely so as to display performance, and so to favour the disputant who has mastered it.

It would be a mistake to conclude that the layperson's position is comfortable. Track records are often unavailable for the questions that matter most, interests can be hidden, and a field can be captured by a fashion that makes its consensus less independent than it appears. The indirect methods narrow the range of reasonable belief; they rarely close it. Still, a choice made on such grounds is not a coin toss, and treating it as one hands an advantage to whoever is most willing to exploit the public's sense of helplessness.

passage: Public debate about bureaucracy tends to oscillate between two complaints. One is that officials are rigid, applying rules mechanically to people whose circumstances the rules never anticipated. The other is that officials are arbitrary, treating similar applicants differently according to mood, prejudice or the length of the queue. The usual remedy for the second complaint is more rules: tighter eligibility criteria, standard forms, checklists that leave nothing to judgement. Each new scandal of favouritism produces another layer of instructions, and the layers accumulate. The remedy is seldom questioned, because it seems obvious that a rule applied uniformly is fairer than a person deciding as he pleases.

What this remedy overlooks is that the officials who deal directly with the public, the benefits clerk, the housing inspector, the teacher deciding which pupil needs extra help, cannot stop exercising judgement however detailed their instructions become. A rule says that an applicant must provide proof of address; it does not say how hard the clerk should look for an acceptable document when the applicant has been living with relatives. Moreover, such officials almost always have more cases than time. They must decide whose file to open first, whose story to probe and whose to accept, and these decisions shape outcomes as surely as any formal ruling. When rules are tightened, judgement does not disappear. It retreats into these less visible choices, where it is harder to observe and correct.

This is not to romanticise frontline discretion. The same latitude that allows a sympathetic clerk to find a way through for a desperate family allows an unsympathetic one to find reasons for delay, and there is ample reason to think that such latitude is not exercised evenly across applicants of different backgrounds. The case for discretion is not that officials can be trusted. It is that the choice is not between discretion and its absence, but between discretion that is acknowledged and discretion that is driven underground. Discretion of the first kind can be examined and improved; discretion of the second kind can only be suspected.

Seen this way, the task of administrative reform changes. Instead of writing rules ever more finely in the hope of closing every gap, an agency might record the informal decisions its staff actually make, review samples of cases to see how similar applicants fare, and give officials explicit guidance on the purposes their judgement should serve. None of these steps would remove judgement from the counter; they would make it something an agency can see, discuss and, where necessary, correct. Such measures concede what the rule-writer prefers to deny: that every system of rules ends, at its edges, in someone deciding.

options.B: After an agency introduces a fixed scoring sheet, its caseworkers come to differ chiefly in how quickly they schedule interviews for the different applicants they serve.
options.C: After an agency introduces a fixed scoring sheet, fewer applicants are approved, because the new sheet is stricter than the assessments it replaced.
